passages.happening:
God now gives the priests his decree. If they will not take it to heart to honor his name, he will send a curse on them and turn even their good things into a curse, and he has already begun (verses 1-2). He will spread on their faces the dung from their feasts (verse 3).

Then he recalls his covenant with Levi, ‘one of life and peace’ (verse 5). Levi revered God. ‘True instruction was in his mouth, and nothing false was found on his lips. He walked with Me in peace and uprightness, and he turned many from iniquity’ (verse 6). ‘For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth, because he is the messenger of the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 7). But these priests have turned aside, and their teaching has caused many to stumble (verse 8). They have shown partiality in matters of the law, so God has made them despised before all the people (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The priests came from the tribe of Levi, and their work went beyond sacrifice. They were to teach the law and judge disputes, so that people came to the priest to learn what God required.

The threat of verse 3 is shocking on purpose. The dung of sacrificial animals was carried outside the camp and burned. Priests who handled holy things would themselves be treated as refuse.

Notice that verse 7 calls the priest the messenger of the LORD, the same word as the prophet's name. A teacher of God's word is a messenger, and a messenger who bends the message for favor misleads the very people who trusted him.
passages.later: In his last words over the tribes, Moses said that Levi would teach Jacob God's ordinances (Deuteronomy 33:10), and God gave the priest Phinehas ‘My covenant of peace’ (Numbers 25:12).
passages.hard:
Why is God's threat against the priests so crude?

Readers are right to notice it. Verse 3 is deliberately offensive. The dung of the sacrifices was refuse, carried outside the camp and burned (Exodus 29:14). The priests had treated God's altar with contempt, and the sentence turns that contempt back on them. It is the language of a prophet trying to wake men who had grown comfortable with holy things.

The warning is aimed at those who teach and lead. It is a sober word for every teacher of God's word: trust given is trust that can be betrayed.
passages.asks: Malachi says a priest's lips should preserve knowledge. Ask what makes a teacher of Scripture trustworthy. And ask who has taught you faithfully, and whether you have thanked them.

passages.happening:
‘Do we not all have one Father? Did not one God create us? Why then do we break faith with one another so as to profane the covenant of our fathers?’ (verse 10). Judah has broken faith by ‘marrying the daughter of a foreign god’ (verse 11). The people weep at the altar because God no longer accepts their offerings, and they ask why (verses 13-14).

‘It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant’ (verse 14). God made them one, and he seeks godly children. ‘So guard yourselves in your spirit and do not break faith with the wife of your youth’ (verse 15). Verse 16 reads in the BSB, “For I hate divorce,” says the LORD, the God of Israel. “He who divorces his wife covers his garment with violence,” says the LORD of Hosts.
passages.hearers:
The same problems appear in Ezra and Nehemiah. Returned exiles, priests and Levites among them, had married women from the surrounding peoples. The concern was not ethnicity as such but worship: these marriages brought other gods into Israelite homes, which the prophets said had led to exile. That is why Malachi speaks of the daughter of a foreign god.

Some men seem to have been divorcing their first wives, perhaps to marry into wealthier families of the land. In a small, poor province such a marriage could bring land, trade and standing. For the wife sent away it could mean poverty and disgrace.

The Old Testament calls marriage a covenant. The wife of your youth is a tender phrase for a first wife married when both were young. Malachi presents the man who discards her as betraying a companion and a covenant partner, with God himself as witness.
passages.later: In the beginning, ‘they will become one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). Nehemiah found men of Judah who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon and Moab (Nehemiah 13:23).
passages.hard:
Does God really hate divorce, and what does it mean for people who have been divorced?

The Hebrew of verse 16 is difficult. Read word by word it says something like for he hates, sending away, and who does the hating is unclear. The BSB and many older translations take God as the subject. Several recent translations take the husband as the subject, so that the verse condemns the man who hates and divorces his wife. The ancient translations also differ. On either reading, the verse condemns a man who discards a faithful wife, and it calls that act violence.

The passage is aimed at men who were breaking covenant, not at those who were abandoned or wronged. Scripture allows divorce in some cases (Deuteronomy 24:1-4; Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15), and Christians differ on exactly which. What Malachi makes plain is that God sees the harm done when vows are broken, and he takes the side of the one betrayed. This passage never asks anyone to stay where they are being harmed.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Verse 10 ties faithfulness to God with faithfulness to one another. Ask where those two go together in your life, and where they have come apart. If you are married, ask what guarding the covenant would look like this week.

passages.t: Where is the God of justice?
passages.happening: ‘You have wearied the LORD with your words’ (verse 17). The people ask how. By saying that all who do evil are good in God's sight and that he delights in them, or by asking, ‘Where is the God of justice?’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The question sounds like faith, but here it is a complaint. The people have decided that God either approves of evildoers or does not care about justice at all. They have seen the arrogant prosper and the faithful struggle, and they have drawn their conclusion.

The verse opens the fourth of the book's six arguments, and it runs straight on into chapter 3. God's answer to where is the God of justice comes in the next verse: he is coming.
passages.later: The psalmist asked the same question and found an answer in God's presence: ‘For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked’ (Psalm 73:3).
passages.asks: The people concluded that God does not care about justice. Ask what you do when it looks as if evildoers prosper. And ask whether your complaint has become a conclusion.
